description: Set, projection, sound and costume choices that build an alternate Britain without naturalistic clutter.
content_html:
Why a Bare Stage?

The RSC premiere of Noughts and Crosses and subsequent tours by Pilot Theatre employed largely minimal staging — a deliberate decision that suits both the play's episodic structure and its political themes. A heavily dressed naturalistic set would anchor the play to one specific time and place, undermining the thought-experiment quality that Blackman's racial reversal requires. If the living room looks exactly like a recognisable 1990s British living room, the audience may not be sufficiently unsettled; if the space is bare and configurable, the familiar is made strange. This is the Brechtian principle of Verfremdungseffekt — estrangement — applied through design.

A designer working on this play must ask: what minimum of physical elements do we need to locate a scene, and what should the rest of the stage communicate about the social world? Every object that remains on stage between scenes says something about the permanence and weight of the system the play depicts.

Key Fact

Minimalist staging in Noughts and Crosses serves the play's political intent: it prevents the audience from becoming comfortable in a recognisable domestic world and keeps focus on relationships and power dynamics rather than period detail. A bare or near-bare set is itself a design argument about what matters in this story.

Set Design: Levels and Symbolic Objects

Even within a minimal approach, a levels structure in the set can carry enormous dramatic meaning. If the Hadley household’s space is positioned upstage on a raised platform while Callum and the nought characters operate at floor level, the architecture of the stage makes the power hierarchy physical before a word is spoken. Designers might use a few key pieces — a chair, a table, a school desk — that are repositioned between scenes to transform the space from domestic to institutional to outdoor.

Props as symbols are particularly important in this play. A school uniform, a set of official papers, handcuffs, or a letter can each carry the weight of the system the play analyses. A designer might make these objects conspicuously plain — functional rather than personalised — to emphasise their institutional nature. The contrast between an impersonal uniform and the warmth of a personal letter reinforces the play’s central tension between state power and individual love.

Four contrasting locations test the designer’s ability to shift from intimacy to institutional power using the same basic materials:

The beach scene — Sephy and Callum as children before the politics intrude. A warm amber lighting state with a soft general wash and perhaps a rippling gobo suggesting water can communicate openness and safety. The stage should feel spacious, the two performers with maximum room between them — and around them — to suggest the freedom of childhood.

The Cross school scene — Callum’s first day, the protest outside. The warmth is replaced by a harder, more frontal white light, suggesting institutional surveillance. The set might narrow with the use of a flat or a row of chairs, reducing the playing area so that Callum physically has less space to occupy — a design metaphor for exclusion.

Prison and interrogation scenes — high contrast lighting, near-blackout backgrounds. A tight profile lantern, hard-edged and white, picks out the figure in a chair while everything else disappears. The absence of set creates claustrophobia more effectively than a detailed prison cell would.

The execution scene — a critical moment of staged public violence. Directors have approached this with great variation. A slow fade to near-darkness, with only a single hanging light source, can make the audience feel the weight of what is about to happen without representing the act in graphic detail. Alternatively, a blackout at the moment of execution, followed by silence, delegates the audience’s imagination to complete the scene.

Lighting Design: Transitions as Narrative

Because the play is episodic, the lighting cross-fade becomes one of the production’s primary storytelling tools. A skilled lighting designer might establish a system of colour associations: warm amber for private moments of hope, cool white-blue for institutional or state power, neutral white for narration. Audiences learn this vocabulary quickly and begin to read the approach of a particular colour as a signal of the scene’s emotional register before the action starts.

Projection can extend the bare stage without adding physical set. Images of newspaper headlines, official notices, or abstract textures projected onto a cyc or back wall can build the world of an alternate Britain. Care is needed: too much projection becomes literal and closes down the audience’s imagination. The most effective use is suggestive — fragmented letters forming a headline, a blurred crowd photograph that could be anywhere, a logo that implies Cross authority without spelling it out.

Costume as Signifier of Hierarchy

Costume design in this play requires careful thinking because the racial hierarchy is expressed through colour and uniform, and a lazy design shortcut — simply dressing Crosses in black and noughts in white — risks reducing the play’s complex thought-experiment to a simplistic binary. A more sophisticated approach might use fabric quality, silhouette and cut to signify the class divide. Cross characters in formal, well-cut clothing — structured fabrics, sharp tailoring — against nought characters in softer, more worn materials communicates hierarchy through the vocabulary of clothing without recourse to a crude colour swap.

The school uniform is a particularly rich design opportunity. It is simultaneously the symbol of Callum’s aspirations (he has been admitted) and of the violence he will face (the school does not truly want him there). A designer might make the Cross school uniform slightly off-fitting on Callum — sleeve lengths wrong, shoes impractical — to suggest that this institutional garment was not made for his body.

Key Fact

Exam answers on costume design must name specific elements: fabric, colour, cut, fit, accessories. “Period costume” or “black and white costumes” will score in the Developing band at best. A strong answer names a specific choice (“the Cross school blazer in deep charcoal wool, crisply pressed, contrasted with the faded, slightly too-large quality of Callum’s jacket as a nought student”) and explains what it communicates to the audience about power and belonging.

A frequently cited student error is to suggest simply dressing Crosses in black and noughts in white (or vice versa) without explaining what specific elements of colour, fabric, fit and uniform signify within the play’s invented hierarchy. The play is not a simple racial swap in its costuming; it is a thought experiment about power, and costume must communicate power through the details of garment construction, maintenance and fit — the same signals that mark class in the real world. Avoid this shortcut. Instead, ask: what does this garment say about who made it, who it was made for, and how much it cost?
exam_tip_html:
For the 8-mark Interpret as Designer question, the single most common error is giving one design idea per discipline (a dark blue light, a sound effect, a plain set) without justifying the choice with reference to what it communicates to the audience at that specific moment. The mark scheme at Mastering level requires concrete, named elements: not ‘dark lighting’ but ‘a 10-degree profile lantern from front-of-house, gelled in a cold Lee 201 full CT blue, picking out the interrogation chair with a hard-edged pool’. Not ‘period costume’ but ‘a charcoal wool blazer, stiff and over-pressed, signalling institutional authority through the rigidity of its fabric’. Every design choice must carry a ‘because’ — what does it make the audience think or feel?

For extended staging questions, avoid trying to design every scene of the play. Focus on one or two named moments in detail — the beach opening, the school scene, the interrogation, the execution — and demonstrate a coherent design language across those moments. Examiners reward a clear and consistent directorial vision, not a list of ideas.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A minimalist set design serves the play’s political thought-experiment by keeping focus on power and relationships rather than period clutter; levels, symbolic props and projection do the work of location without naturalistic decoration.
  • Lighting cross-fades and colour associations — a system of warm amber for intimacy, cold blue for institutional power — become the primary storytelling tools in an episodic play, and every state must be justified by its effect on the audience at that named moment.
  • Costume must communicate hierarchy through fabric quality, cut and fit rather than a simple colour swap; the school uniform scene is a key opportunity to show how a garment communicates belonging or exclusion through its construction and how it fits the body wearing it.

practice_questions.text: Name one staging configuration that would suit Noughts and Crosses and briefly state why.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one named configuration (end-on / proscenium arch / thrust / in-the-round / traverse) with a brief justification (e.g. 'end-on because it allows projection onto a back wall and focuses the audience on the two narrators at downstage centre').

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'Verfremdungseffekt' in the context of theatre design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that it means making familiar things strange or creating a sense of estrangement; 1 mark for explaining that this is associated with Brecht and is used to provoke critical thinking rather than emotional immersion in the audience.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of using projection in Noughts and Crosses. In your answer, refer to a specific moment when this design element could be used and explain how it affects the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identifying projection as a world-building device on a bare stage (1), explaining that it can communicate news, authority or location without physical set (1), explaining the specific effect on the audience at a named moment (e.g. fragmented newspaper headlines during the school scene suggesting Cross media bias) (1), explaining how this projection choice reinforces the play's political message (1).

practice_questions.text: As a lighting designer, explain how you would design the lighting for two contrasting scenes in Noughts and Crosses: the beach scene in which Sephy and Callum meet as children and the interrogation scene. For each scene, name specific lighting elements and explain their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): both scenes addressed with specific, named lighting elements for each; beach scene: named warm colour (e.g. Lee 103 straw or amber gel), broad wash, possibly a ripple gobo suggesting water, spacious positioning of lanterns to suggest openness; interrogation scene: hard-edged profile lantern, cold white or blue gel, tight pool isolating a single chair, high contrast to create claustrophobia; for each scene, a clear explanation of the effect on the audience (warmth and freedom vs surveillance and confinement); choices are concrete (lantern type, gel colour or number, angle, spread).
Secure (5-6): both scenes addressed with generally appropriate choices; at least one specific element per scene; effect on audience identified if not fully developed.
Developing (3-4): relevant ideas but generic (warm light for beach, dark for prison); limited specificity; effect on audience implied.
Emerging (1-2): basic identification of lighting with little or no justification; may describe only one scene.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the playwright's and director's intentions in choosing a largely bare stage for Noughts and Crosses. What do you think this staging choice communicates to the audience about the world of the play?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): sustained analysis linking the bare stage to the play's Brechtian intent and thought-experiment quality; argues that a naturalistic set would anchor the play too firmly in a recognisable world, undermining its estrangement effect; at least two named scenes discussed with specific staging implications; considers how different elements (levels, symbolic props, projection) take over from physical set; substantiated judgement about the cumulative effect on the audience's critical engagement.
Secure (7-9): clear analysis of intentions with reference to the play's political or Brechtian dimension; at least one named scene; generally accurate effect identified; some specific staging elements discussed.
Developing (4-6): relevant but largely descriptive; may explain that bare stage is practical rather than political; limited named moments; effect on audience implied.
Emerging (1-3): basic point that the stage is bare with little or no analysis of why or what this communicates.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how you would design the set, lighting and costume for the Cross school scene in Noughts and Crosses, in which Callum arrives on his first day. Explain how each design choice communicates the power dynamics between Callum as a nought student and the Cross school environment, and what effect you want these choices to have on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (17-20): detailed and coherent design vision covering set (how the space is configured to make Callum physically smaller or more exposed; use of levels; institutional furniture), lighting (named lanterns and gels, hard-edged surveillance quality, colour contrast with earlier warm scenes), and costume (specific fabric and fit details for Callum's uniform vs Cross students' uniforms, communicating exclusion through material quality and fit); every choice anchored to the named scene and justified by its effect on the audience; consistent directorial vision; substantiated conclusions about cumulative audience response to the design as a whole.
Secure (12-16): all three design areas addressed with at least one specific choice per area; generally accurate staging logic; named moment referenced; some justification of choices in terms of audience effect.
Developing (7-11): relevant ideas across at least two design areas; generic terminology in places; limited justification; effects implied.
Emerging (1-6): basic design suggestions with little technical vocabulary; may drift into plot retelling rather than design analysis.

A lighting effect using coloured gels
Making familiar things seem strange to provoke critical thought, associated with Brecht
A method of projecting images onto a back wall

knowledge_checks.q: Why might a designer choose a minimalist set for Noughts and Crosses?
options: Because the production budget is very low
To prevent the audience becoming comfortable in a recognisable domestic world, keeping focus on power dynamics
Because the script specifies no set at all
Because naturalistic sets are always wrong for school drama productions

knowledge_checks.q: A sudden, complete darkening of the stage is called a _____.
In exam answers, costume design for Noughts and Crosses should reference specific _____, _____ and _____ rather than simply suggesting black and white costumes.
Match each design element to its primary function in Noughts and Crosses:
right: Communicates hierarchy physically before a word is spoken
Builds the world of an alternate Britain without adding physical set
Transitions between scenes and signals shifts in emotional register

flashcard_questions.a: Brecht's technique of making the familiar seem strange to provoke critical thinking rather than emotional immersion.
The overall illumination level and colour on stage at any given point, set by the lighting designer.
A gradual change from one lighting state to another, with both briefly visible at the same time.

flashcard_questions.q: What is meant by 'levels' in set design?
flashcard_questions.a: Platforms, rostra or steps that create varying heights, allowing directors to communicate hierarchy and focus.
Objects used on stage that carry symbolic significance beyond their practical function.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is a simple black-and-white costume scheme insufficient for Noughts and Crosses?
flashcard_questions.a: It reduces the play's complex thought-experiment to a crude binary; fabric, cut and fit communicate hierarchy more precisely.

flashcard_questions.q: What design choice could a lighting designer use for the interrogation scene?
flashcard_questions.a: A hard-edged profile lantern, cold gel, tight pool on a single chair — high contrast, minimal fill light.
A sudden, complete darkening of the stage.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the episodic structure of Noughts and Crosses place special demands on lighting design?
flashcard_questions.a: Lighting cross-fades must carry the work of scene transitions, building a colour language audiences read across the whole production.
A performance style in which the set, costume and acting aim to represent everyday life as realistically as possible.
A deliberate departure from realism, using exaggerated, symbolic or abstract elements to communicate meaning.
A hard-edged spotlight that can be focused to a precise beam shape; used for specials and tight area lighting.

glossary_terms.definition: Brecht's technique of making familiar things seem strange in order to provoke critical thought in the audience rather than emotional immersion.
The overall illumination level and colour on stage at any given point, controlled by the lighting designer.
A gradual transition from one lighting state to another, with both states briefly visible simultaneously.
Platforms, rostra, steps or ramps in a set design that create varying heights, used to communicate hierarchy and focus.
Objects used on stage that carry symbolic significance beyond their practical function, conveying theme or character.
A sudden, complete darkening of the stage, used to signal the end of a scene or a moment of dramatic impact.
A performance style in which set, costume and acting aim to represent everyday life as realistically as possible.
A deliberate departure from realism, using exaggerated, symbolic or abstract elements to communicate meaning.
